section_summary: This section traces the tightening and politicization of Japanese press controls from late 1930 through July 1936. It covers the press protest arising from the detention of a Jiji Shimpo reporter, extensive bans concealing military operations and developments in Manchuria, attempts to suppress inflammatory writing, and growing government control of newspapers, correspondents, translators, and news agencies. The closing documents concern the consolidation of Domei Tsushinsha, restrictions on foreign information gathering, and Japan's suppression of the May 1936 issue of Current History.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 96: Press protest against police interference
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the political controversy caused by the detention and interrogation of Jiji Shimpo reporter Hosokoshi.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo newspapers jointly protested after police used Hosokoshi's detention to seek information about General Ugaki's political ambitions and relations with Baron Tanaka. The press resolution denounced censorship, political spying, and intimidation, while Ugaki and the Privy Council also criticized the police. Home Minister Adachi apologized and promised respect for press freedom, but the affair damaged his political position and may have influenced Shidehara's decision to continue as acting prime minister.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram on strict press censorship
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to a telegram concerning strict censorship of the press and correspondents.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to telegram 77 (file 793.94/4380) on strict censorship of the press and correspondents in Japan.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 76: Government crisis, Shanghai deployments, and censorship
subfiles.about: Reports rumors of a Japanese government change, additional troop deployments to Shanghai, and strict news censorship.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 76: Forbes reports financial difficulties and military influence raising rumors of a coalition cabinet despite the government party's victory, two more divisions going to Shanghai, Major Bratton's and Lieutenant Dusenbury's movements reflecting military planning, and strict censorship hampering news.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram on Manchurian troop-movement bans
subfiles.about: Refers to a telegram concerning press bans on Japanese troop movements to Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to telegram 164 (file 893.01-Manchuria/280) on suppression of news of Japanese troops moving to Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum on Tokyo despatch No. 48
subfiles.about: Recommends reading Tokyo's despatch and its classified list of press bans.
subfiles.summary: Memo: Despatch 48 encloses bans on Japanese and foreign newspapers in Tokyo since September 18, 1931, with analysis of restrictions on troop and naval movements, Manchuria and social problems.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 48: Analysis of Japanese press bans
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits and analyzes confidential lists of press bans imposed in Tokyo since the Manchurian Incident.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 48: Grew sorts the bans into troop and naval movements, Manchurian affairs and civil disturbances, concluding they hid frontier defenses, reinforcements, Japan's role in Manchukuo and plans for communications, finance and a permanent garrison, though some foreign correspondents still sent banned news abroad.

subfiles.title: Enclosure: Chronological lists of press bans
subfiles.about: Lists individual Japanese press bans issued from September 1931 through June 1932.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure records restrictions on troop and naval movements, including operations toward Shanghai, Manchuria, Sakhalin, and Korea. Other bans concealed Japanese involvement in Manchukuo, communications and financial policy, political violence, the May 15 Incident, leftist activity, agricultural distress, and banking conditions. Several entries also record when particular bans were partly or wholly lifted.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 219: Press bans involving Jehol, Sakhalin, and Manchukuo
subfiles.about: Reports three current press bans and the expected timing of Japanese recognition of Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 219: bans cover reporting on Jehol and troop movements, destroyers sent to Sakhalin and treaty talks with Manchukuo; Grew expects the Privy Council to pass the treaty around September 20 with recognition soon after.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to letter on the anti-American press campaign
subfiles.about: Refers to a letter describing an organized Japanese press campaign against the United States.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a letter: the anti-American press campaign seemed centrally stimulated, with almost nothing favorable to the U.S. permitted.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 39: Ban on military and naval deployment information
subfiles.about: Reports new censorship orders covering forces destined for China and Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 39: the main ban covers the identity, strength and movement of warships, aircraft and units to be sent from Japan, plus experimental aircraft, Manchuria and Jehol plans, and arrests of General Li's emissaries at Benxi; only Navy-released information may be published.

subfiles.title: Department analysis of telegram No. 39
subfiles.about: Assesses the legal and military significance of the reported censorship order.
subfiles.summary: Memo: Article 27 of the Press Law already let the War and Navy Ministers restrict military reporting; the new orders perfect control and put the press on a wartime basis, and since similar bans preceded operations, large movements may be imminent.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram No. 61
subfiles.about: Refers to a telegram about the March 9 ban on reporting forces destined for China or Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: The sheet repeats the central language of the military and naval press ban. It links the document to file 793.94/6037.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 61: Press ban preceding possible operations
subfiles.about: Connects a March 9 military press ban with the prospect of renewed operations.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 61: Grew reports publication banned on warships, aircraft or unit strength expected to go from Japan to China or Manchukuo; similar bans previously preceded active operations.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram on Manchukuo–North China negotiations
subfiles.about: Refers to a telegram reporting a ban on comment about negotiations between Manchukuo and North China.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to telegram 168 in the Manchuria file on the ban on commenting on current Manchukuo-North China negotiations.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 168: Ban on comment about North China negotiations
subfiles.about: Reports a press ban concerning negotiations between Manchukuo and the North China administration.
subfiles.summary: The ban forbade comment on the negotiations. The Embassy had no additional information and repeated the message to Peiping.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram on inflammatory publications
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Foreign Office initiative to prevent provocative books and articles.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: a January 23 interministerial meeting on publications predicting war or endangering foreign relations; the Foreign Office would stop a book then in production.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 18: Plans to prohibit inflammatory books and articles
subfiles.about: Reports an interministerial effort to restrict writings that presaged war or harmed international relations.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 18: Foreign, War, Navy and Home Ministry representatives met January 23 on stopping provocative publications by retired officers and others; the Foreign Office told Grew a book already on the press would be prevented.

subfiles.title: Japanese Embassy letter transmitting Hirota's policy message
subfiles.about: Transmits an English translation of a telegram from Foreign Minister Hirota on suppressing harmful publications.
subfiles.summary: Saito says he discussed the issue with the President at luncheon and believed him strongly interested; the enclosed translation conveys Japan's decision to suppress writings harmful to foreign relations.

subfiles.title: Translation of Japanese decision on harmful publications
subfiles.from: Kōki Hirota, Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.to: Hiroshi Saitō, Japanese Ambassador in Washington
subfiles.about: Sets out two categories of publications the Japanese Government intended to suppress.
subfiles.summary: Translation of Japan's decision on harmful publications: works revealing or imagining Japanese tactics in a foreign war, or asserting war with a country is necessary or inevitable, or exciting foreign opinion.

subfiles.title: Department reading memorandum on inflammatory publications
subfiles.about: Recommends Grew's despatch on Japan's growing concern over inflammatory writing.
subfiles.summary: Memo mentions Counts Futara's and Soejima's recent travels, suggesting Futara got useful ideas abroad, and directs attention to the Foreign Office statement on regulating publications affecting international relations.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 684: Inflammatory publications
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Describes Diet criticism of warlike publications and the government's promise of stricter control.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 684: Count Futara, War Minister Hayashi, Jinjiro Mizuno and Yoshizawa warned imaginary-war stories and provocative books hurt diplomacy; Grew notes they sold widely and were often military-inspired, though the military now thought propaganda went too far; the Foreign Office promised stricter censorship.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum on the Japan Advertiser
subfiles.about: Provides background on the finances and independence of the Japan Advertiser before presenting reports on news control.
subfiles.summary: Memo: after the 1923 earthquake, Lamont, Rockefeller and Crane funded B. W. Fleisher to rebuild an independent American-oriented paper; after a 1930 fire Fleisher refused Japanese financing via Takuma Dan and Finance Minister Inoue fearing obligations, and would close the paper rather than accept a subsidy.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 955: Control of news by the Japanese Government
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits differing foreign-correspondent assessments of increasing Japanese control over news.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 955: Grew reports complaints from Wilfred Fleisher and James Young, while AP's Glenn Babb thought censorship reasonable; all saw planned news-agency consolidation as preparing tighter control for the 1935-36 crisis, and Grew wondered whether his anti-inflammatory efforts encouraged intervention.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 1: Statement by Wilfred Fleisher
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, recording Wilfred Fleisher's statement
subfiles.about: Records pressure on the foreign-owned Japan Advertiser to adopt a more cooperative position toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: Wilfred Fleisher describes Shigeru Yoshida's merger suggestion, Eiji Amau's criticism and threatened South Manchuria Railway and Mitsui ad cuts; official tolerance of foreign reporting is narrowing; the paper rejected a tentative subsidy and prefers closure to losing independence.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 2: Statement by James R. Young
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, recording James R. Young's statement
subfiles.about: Records Young's view that restrictions and official pressure on foreign reporting had recently increased.
subfiles.summary: James Young says Japanese sources grew reticent after reprimands and the Foreign Office rebuked him over stories; he asserts much press material, including claims about American activity in China, comes from the War Office, Japan's most active propaganda factory.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram on the Manchurian oil monopoly
subfiles.about: Refers to a telegram reporting suppression of news about the proposed Manchurian oil monopoly.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to telegram 236 on a Japanese ban on publishing news of the Manchurian oil monopoly.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 236: Manchurian oil monopoly and the open door
subfiles.about: Reports Eiji Amau's statements on Manchukuo and a press ban covering the proposed oil monopoly.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 236: Amau reportedly says protests should go to Manchukuo or China, the Nine-Power Treaty doesn't apply and open-door declarations can be withdrawn; a press ban barred direct reporting on the oil monopoly, though papers mentioned Washington and London representations.

subfiles.title: Report No. 292: Censorship of newspapers
subfiles.about: Assesses the severity and uneven operation of Japanese newspaper censorship, especially over naval information.
subfiles.summary: Report 292: the four ministries can impose one of the world's strictest censorships; naval reporting is so vague papers sometimes invent policy news, bans fall harder on Tokyo and Osaka dailies than provincial papers, and almost no useful military information would appear in wartime.

subfiles.title: Department reading note on cartoons of chiefs of state
subfiles.about: Recommends Grew's short despatch on caricatures of foreign leaders in Japanese newspapers.
subfiles.summary: Reading note drawing attention to Despatch 1626 on cartoons of chiefs of state in the Japanese press.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1626: Cartoons of chiefs of state
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits Japanese newspaper cartoons after protests over a Vanity Fair depiction of the Japanese emperor.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 1626: Grew, citing people in glass houses, sends examples of Japanese treatment of foreign leaders; after a German protest over Hitler caricatures the Interior Ministry reportedly ordered no caricatures of foreign sovereigns, widely disregarded.

subfiles.title: Kokumin clipping on Roosevelt's congressional message
subfiles.about: Reports President Roosevelt's warning that worsening international affairs could produce a great war.
subfiles.summary: Kokumin clipping: its translated headline stresses Roosevelt's fear that unfavorable international trends might lead to general war, summarizing his message to Congress.

subfiles.title: Yomiuri clipping on Hitler and an aerial Locarno pact
subfiles.about: Uses a hostile headline to describe Hitler's reported conditions for joining an aerial Locarno agreement.
subfiles.summary: Yomiuri clipping on Hitler and an aerial Locarno pact: calls him overbearing, demanding Europe's strongest air force and former colonies, illustrating the provocative treatment in Grew's despatch.

subfiles.title: Jiji Shimpo clipping on Hitler's reported demands
subfiles.about: Reports that Hitler's firm position had obstructed negotiations over an aerial Locarno agreement.
subfiles.summary: Jiji Shimpo clipping: headlines call Hitler's terms brazen demands and say the agreement hit a snag, with a British denial of new demands.

subfiles.title: Department summary of increased control of news
subfiles.about: Summarizes Embassy despatch No. 1775 on new Japanese controls over news collection and distribution.
subfiles.summary: Summary: the government-sponsored merger of Nippon Dempo into Domei Tsushinsha creates a vehicle for the approved Japanese version; police suppressed the Okayama translation service, arrested Soviet and Chinese Embassy translators, and pressured correspondents; diplomatic and consular information gathering will be much harder.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1775: Increased control of news in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Provides a comprehensive report on government efforts to control news agencies, translators, correspondents, and foreign information gathering.
subfiles.summary: Grew describes the forced amalgamation of Nippon Dempo with the partly official Domei Tsushinsha, predicting that it would distribute approved domestic and international propaganda and restrict incoming foreign news. Police closed the Okayama translation service and arrested translators employed by the Soviet and Chinese Embassies, apparently to obstruct the flow of information. The despatch also covers censorship of foreign correspondents, Gerald Sampson's arrest and deportation, proposed controls on commercial information, and expanded surveillance of foreigners. Grew concludes that measures directed mainly against Soviet organizations would also impede other diplomatic missions and news agencies.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch No. 1876 on press restriction bills
subfiles.about: Refers to a report on restrictions created by the Seditious Literature and Mobilization Secrets bills.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to despatch 1876 (file 894.20/166) on legislation further restricting the Japanese press.

subfiles.title: Current History inquiry about suppression of its May issue
subfiles.about: Requests information about Japan's suppression of the May 1936 issue of Current History.
subfiles.summary: Casman says the New York post office told Current History its May issue was suppressed in Japan; he encloses mention of a communication to Japan's Ambassador and asks for any explanation.

subfiles.title: Department acknowledgment of Current History inquiry
subfiles.from: Wilbur J. Carr for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the magazine's inquiry and promises an Embassy investigation.
subfiles.summary: Carr says State had only newspaper reports of the suppression and asked the Tokyo Embassy to find and report the facts.

subfiles.title: Instruction to investigate the Current History ban
subfiles.about: Orders the Embassy to investigate suppression of the May issue of Current History.
subfiles.summary: Instruction asks the Embassy to ascertain the facts of the Current History ban and return the report through naval radio at Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Washington Times clipping: Japan seizes magazines
subfiles.about: Reports the confiscation at Kobe of copies of Current History's May issue.
subfiles.summary: Washington Times clipping: Kobe postal authorities apparently seized the magazine because of articles on Japanese affairs; publisher M. E. Tracy sought explanations from State and the Japanese Embassy.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum on the Current History inquiry
subfiles.about: Clarifies the relationship between Current History's letter and the Washington Times report.
subfiles.summary: Michael McDermott says State received no inquiry beyond the magazine's July 14 letter and believes the July 20 Washington Times item referred to it.

subfiles.title: Relayed Tokyo telegram on the Current History ban
subfiles.from: Clarence E. Gauss, Shanghai, relaying Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the Embassy's findings on why Current History's May issue was denied distribution.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo telegram: the local distributor was officially told the issue couldn't circulate, naming no article; foreign publications are routinely banned this way; Embassy inquiries suggest February 26 Incident references triggered the ban, unverified.

subfiles.title: Department's final reply to Current History
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Provides the magazine with the Embassy's explanation for suppression of its May issue.
subfiles.summary: Welles tells Current History the Japanese agent was ordered not to distribute the issue without being told which article offended; it apparently discussed the February 26 Incident, which police had banned, so State believed the suppression lawful under Japanese law.
